I don't have the reference in front of me, but in the Milosevic proceedings, I believe you had testified that you were not certain whether you had reported the -- the discovery of the bodies in the house, and you yesterday testified that you had in fact reported it to your unit or ceta, commander. Do you in fact actually know whether you reported that and a report was generated, or do you not know whether in fact a report was generated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the previous trial and in this trial, I said that we informed the company commander about the incidents, but I can't remember exactly when, whether it was on the same day or the following day, because the man was constantly going back and forth across our positions, and he was not always there with us. But I know that he also informed the commander of the 23rd detachment in writing. And when, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, with -- I asked this question because yesterday, the Trial Chamber was interested in the precise date that you were -- that you ceased your employment with the MUP. With -- I don't need to go -- know all the details of your employment, but am I correct that your -- the cessation of your employment within the MUP was not in any way tied to your testifying in the Milosevic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify? Was it -- was your cessation of employment within the MUP tied to your testimony in the Milosevic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, when you were first approached by the Prosecutors of this Tribunal, isn't it a fact that you actually advised your police superiors and reported them -- reported to them that in fact you were speaking with the Prosecutor's office? That is to say, it was not -- it was not a secret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not. I informed them also in 1999 when that journalist contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, specifically with respect to your discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor, isn't it correct that the Serbian MUP and the Serbian authorities gave you the authorisation to talk freely with the Office of the Prosecutor and even excused you from having to keep any state secrets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sir, I thank you for assisting me here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm completed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask a few questions by way of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, well, I can't really address you with a K and a number, but let us try and move on. My name is Toma Fila and I wanted to assist you in trying to clarify the call-ups in Serbia and Kosovo in times of peace and war. I wanted to ask you this: What are the criteria when the reserve is being mobilised? For example, when you were after that serial killer, who was called up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we were after him there was no call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the criteria, then, when you are called up in peacetime to serve with the reserves? What sort of a person is being called up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without any criminal offences and convictions, and with at least a high school degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This means that it is being carefully considered as to who will be chosen so that they wouldn't disregard the dignity of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And some inquiries would usually be made at his working place and with the neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But there was a difference with Kosovo, so can you explain to us what type of people were called up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local Serbs, because they were the only ones who were able to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the criteria by that time were gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we use this to explain the three people mentioned and that these people had no respect for the uniforms such as the one you had and the people in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We might say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, counsel for General Lazarevic. My learned friends basically exhausted all the topics I was interested in, but there is one left and I will have a few questions for you. In your statement and yesterday during examination-in-chief, you stated that in the second half of 1998 the only operation in which VJ support was provided to your unit was the MUP operation in Junik. First of all, I'd like to know whether it is correct if I say that Junik is 5 to 6 kilometres away from the state border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is also correct that the closest border post is Kosare, which on several occasions was taken by the Albanian terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Am I also correct in assuming that Junik, at the time of the operation, was one of the major strongholds, well-fortified, of the Albanian terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Am I also correct to assume that at the time of the operation there were over 1.000 Albanian terrorists in Junik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were supposed to have been around 3.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Having in mind the facts you've just confirmed and having in mind the figure, and the fact that this was an important stronghold, am I right in saying that the howitzer support from the Radonjic Lake was very necessary to break the resistance and to secure the state border towards Albania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were supported for 21 days by four tanks as well, and this was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, for 21 days, this is how long the combat lasted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My last question is this: Did you know, sir, that after that operation in Junik foreign diplomats toured Junik and verified the results of the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just a couple of issues. Going back to the issue of civilian vehicles being used. On page 12 of your statement, you talk about the trucks and buses that were used to transport away the civilian population from the area, and you state there that these were civilian trucks and buses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When our company set out, the vehicles were given to us for use, but issues -- certificates were issued, so the company took over the vehicles and we were able to use them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think we talked about two different kinds of vehicles now. You're talking about the vehicles that brought you into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the statement as well I describe that we received civilian vehicles from the ministry of the interior, and they were provided by various state and private companies. They did not have -- have any Ministry of the Interior insignia, but they were used for our needs, and that could have taken place anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's helpful. But I was actually referring to the buses that came to help transport out the civilians out of the combat zone, and I just want to clarify whether we understand correctly that these buses only came after you and your unit called the SUP Prizren about the huge number of -- of refugees that were arriving at the location and that these buses that were then sent were indeed civilian vehicles as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first information of the arrival of refugees was received by the Prizren SUP. They told us where we should concentrate them, and they said they would provide transport. We put them all at the train station in Velika and Mala Krusa, and then we provided transport on civilian buses. They were manned by reserve policemen and professional policemen, and there were also some people in civilian clothes as well as some of the people in our uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you explained further in your statement that the police had actually in this situation the right to commandeer civilian vehicles and use them for such operations, right, and that this was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I've explained that as part of the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the VJ would have the same right to commandeer vehicles, would they, in this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only assume that it is so, but I am not certain. In times of war, this is possible, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, going to the questions of the insignias worn on PJP uniforms. The issue was raised that PJP policemen would be easily distinguishable from the insignias. We looked at the insignia yesterday in Exhibit P1323. Where was this badge that we looked at, where would this badge be located on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the left and the right side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And approximately how big was such a badge in terms of centimetres or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Say 15 or 20 centimetres. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were there any other insignia that you would wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you say in your statement on page 15 in relation to the incident where you encountered these policemen who were trying to rob civilians, that your commander on this occasion wore his ranks but that he didn't wear them all the time. So would you wear your insignia all the time, or would you also in combat situations wear different kinds of insignia or less than in other situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, it is not the question of our insignia but of rank. Snipers were going for high -- higher-ranking officers. That's why we did not wear rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So it was usual that higher-ranking officers would not be recognisable as such because they would not always wear their ranks in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of us wore any rank insignia. And actually, we took them off. They were unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, we -- my learned colleague Mr. Ivetic also talked with you about the role and the function of the PJP and the kind of training that you received. Is it correct that the people who delivered the training to the PJP included VJ military personnel as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And is it also correct -- were you also instructed on the use of specific weapons that would usually used only in combat situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you state which kind of weapons you were trained at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anti-personnel mines, the Wasp and Zolja rocket launchers and the Browning machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So would it be logical to draw the inference from this training that to participate in combat operations was also one of the roles of the PJP that was envisaged for such units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked questions about civilians leaving the area of the operation and whether any documents were taken from such people. You say in your statement that you saw approximately 5.000 people or even more passing through this main road during the time you were deployed in this area; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you had the instruction to hand these people over to the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then they would take further care of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So do you actually know what happened to these people after you -- you handed them over to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know they were transported by buses, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you know where they were transported to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was in the direction of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. So you cannot say whether at any later point actually documents were taken from these people, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You also say in your statement, and it's page 11 in the English version, that you heard stories about forcible removal of people and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. I think I have to object. I don't think that the statement is what is the subject of redirect. I think what was in the cross-examination that would have to be the subject of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, what's the issue that arises from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The issue is people were possibly expelled, and I think Mr. Ackerman asked the witness in the beginning of his cross-examination whether he ever recognised people being forcibly expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's not exactly right. I asked him if he ever did that, and he said he didn't. And if he saw anyone doing it would he report it, and he said he would. That's exactly what I asked and what was answered. I don't think that's raised, this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the Prosecution are entitled to clarify the issue that Ms. Moeller identifies. I don't think the way to do it is immediately in asking the witness about the issue to direct his attention to his statement. Let's have open questions in re-examination and then if necessary the statement can be used to confront him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, did you talk to -- did you talk to some of the civilians of these 5.000 civilians that passed along the street during the time you were there? For instance, when you organised to have them given water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did they tell you how -- how they came to be there in the location where you met them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told different stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what kind of stories would they tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we forced them out, that the KLA attacked them, that they were being bombed. They were telling all sorts of stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, another question put to you in cross-examination concerned the reserve forces, and you -- that was when my learned colleague Mr. Fila asked you, and you gave an answer to the extent saying only local Serbs could help, could be part of the reserve forces in Kosovo. Why couldn't loyal non-Serbs and any other ethnicities living in Kosovo be called up into the reserve, which I understood was also part of -- called up partly to prepare for a potential NATO attack? Why couldn't they be in the local reserve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were not considered as being trustworthy. They couldn't have been engaged by our side. And they also asked not to be. There was not a single loyal Albanian who could have said, "Please, do mobilise me," at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Another issue raised was the issue of people putting on uniforms of a unit they didn't belong to. Did you ever notice or know about Serb forces sometimes putting on KLA uniforms in operations to get closer to them in a strategic way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, the last issue. You were asked about some events shortly after you were contacted for the first time by the Tribunal. After the Tribunal contacted you and wanted you to testify here the first time, were you ever called in a meeting where representatives (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who called that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1999, they asked me to come once I had told them that I was contacted by journalists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can you describe how that meeting went along? Who was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I rather wouldn't, if I may refuse to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we maybe go into private session, and the witness may be able to tell us more about this event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your reason for refusing to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no reasons. I will reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to do so in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session because the witness seems concerned about his security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is K24, also a protected witness who will be handled in closed session with a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when the court resumes after this break, we will resume in closed session with the witness already in place. All right. So thank you, K25, for your evidence. The Court will now rise and resume again at 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.14 p.m.,
